My hon.' friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) asked on two or three successive days for information in regard to the embargo on the export of oats and oatmeal. I gave him some information, and now I will give the whole of it. Oats are prohibited to all destinations other than the United Kingdom and British possessions and protectorates, France, Russia (except Baltic ports), Italy, Japan and the United States for home consumption, or when shipped to designated consignees in the United Kingdom via United States. Rolled oats and oatmeal are prohibited to all foreign ports in Europe, and on the Mediterranean and Black seas other than those of France, Russia (except Baltic ports), Belgium, Spain, Portugal and Italy. Rolled oats and oatmeal cannot be shipped to Holland. Wheat, wheat flour, barley and rye may be shipped when consigned to the Netherlands Government or to the Netherlands Overseas Trust. There is nothing, however, to prevent shipments to a United States agent, and thence to Holland. The Quaker Oats people desired a permit to ship oatmeal to Holland, but they have not been successful.

speechtext:
I desire to place the following before the House:
Memorandum regarding disturbance at Berlin,
Ont., on Tuesday night, February 15, 1916.
The oral report received from the Officer Commanding is as follows:
1.	For some time the feeling of loyal and law-abiding citizens of both British and German extraction in Berlin and Waterloo and adjoining localities, have been more or less exasperated by the language and actions of a Lutheran clergyman-an American citizen named Cap-pert-and by a German born Canadian subject named Asmussen, who, whether with good or bad intent, have been semi-apologists for German atrocities and Kaiserism. It is asserted that one of these men has recently stated that ' the conduct of the British, in the war, has been about as bad as the conduct of the Germans.' It has not been specifically charged that these utterances have been made with disloyal intent, but merely as seeking not to justify German brutality as much as to condone it. These utterances, coupled with the general tension of mind throughout the country over the war, gradually wrought up a number of people to a high pitch of feeling.
2.	On Sunday last, a young man who had been behind the German lines for some months, as a reporter for an American journal, and who had personally witnessed these horrible atrocities, spoke in Waterloo and Berlin, and in vigorous terms denounced the spirit and recent utterances of the two men above named.
3.	The feeling already highly strung on the part of many, found vent on Tuesday evening when ten or fifteen young soldiers, heard that German flags were displayed in a hall in Berlin. They quietly assembled near the place
about nine o'clock in the evening, and in the course of a very few minutes had torn the German flags to pieces, while a bust of the former Kaiser William I was carried along the street. There were five policemen within easy call on the street, but the affair seems to have been over so quickly that they did not get time to interfere.
4.	Colonel Lochead, on receiving a telephone message at the barracks, immediately repaired to the locality, when order was promptly restored.
I may add further that an inquiry is being held. The civil authorities are also acting in the premises. The authorities have been fully informed that soldiers in uniform lose none of their rights or responsibilities as citizens, and therefore are entitled to all the privileges of the law, but are also subject to its penalties. On the other hand, it will be observed that alien enemies have been treated by the Canadian Government in the most tolerant and lenient manner; but utterances and conduct that even indirectly encourage sedition, treason, or disloyalty, will not be tolerated.
The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) brought up a matter concerning Campbellton to which I referred yesterday. I have the facts, as stated by the officer in command, Colonel Mersereau, who says that on no occasion since the troops have been in Campbellton have there been more than four men locked up or impounded, or under supervision, in any one day, out of 290 men present. I merely add without comment that we hear all sorts of stories about the volunteers. We hear that the men of the 77th battalion in Ottawa looted the Parliament Buildings the night of the fire. I am prepared to say this-I never thought it worth while mentioning it, but my attention was brought to it yesterday-that the men of the 77th, as well as the Engineers, conducted themselves in the most orderly and becoming manner on that night; they worked throughout the entire night, and many of them through the following day, performing guard duty, and removing furniture and other articles from the Parliament Buildings, and I have yet to learn of one specific instance of any thing unbecoming a soldier and a gentleman having been done by any soldier of the 77th or any engineer on that occasion.

The House resumed, from Monday, February 14, consideration of the proposed resolution of Mr. Turriff:
That in the opinion of this House, in order to secure to the farmers and people of Canada the advantages of the American market for wheat products and potatoes, steps should be taken at once to put these articles on the free list in the Canadian Tariff.

Mr. Speaker, this question of free wheat, as it is called, is the second big question before the House at the present time. The object of the resolution is to obtain free 
entrance to the American market for our wheat. In order to get our wheat to the American market free of duty, all this Government has to do is to remove the protection of ten cents a bushel which the Canadian wheat grower is supposed to enjoy, but which he does not want. Of course, the supreme question before us at the present time is the war. This question of free wheat comes a long way behind, but at the same time it is a matter of great importance to the West; and, as it will mean greater purchasing power for our western farmers,, it is of great importance to the country as a whole.
There are two or three points to be considered:	First, would free entrance
to the American market mean a better price for our farmers; and, second-and this is more important than the first-would it relieve the congestion which always obtains in the West whenever there is a big crop? Light crops the railway companies can handle very well; but when there is a large crop there is always congestion; heaps of grain are left in the fields during the winter, and not taken away until perhaps the following spring, when some of it is spoiled. But I am not going into that phase, as the mover of the resolution has already dealt with it very fully. Another question to be answered is: would free wheat affect the revenue of this country? I think we can answer that by saying that it would not, for very little wheat is imported into this country from the United States; a certain quantity, however, is always imported no matter how much we export. The United States is a great exporter of wheat, but there are different kinds of wheat. For instance, I think our Northwest is the only part of the world, with the exception of a couple of the Northern States, and perhaps Northern Russia, that can produce hard wheat. The United States exports no hard wheat. Our hard wheat is, therefore, at a premium, and will continue to be so, I think.
In spite of the facts to the contrary, an opponent of free wheat occasionally appears with the statement that, on the average, prices of grain are higher at Winnipeg than at Minneapolis. In order to remove any doubt on this matter, the following figures have been compiled, showing the cash prices of No. 1 Northern wheat at Winnipeg and Minneapolis on the last day of each week in November and December, 1911, and for the years 1912, 1913, 1914 and 1915, as given on the market page of the Guide from week to

week. These are not political figures, but are culled from the market reports. As they are rather lengthy, I would ask the permission of the House to have them placed on Hansard without being read.

In the early days of the crop movement the spread between the cash price for wheat in Minneapolis and Winnipeg in favour of the former market was very noticeable, but as the season advanced the heavy premiums for prompt delivery at the lake terminals gradually wiped out the difference and for a short time put Winnipeg in the premier position as to price, with the close of navigation, however, the spread reappeared, and it has been widening until yesterday No. 1 Northern was worth 81 cents a bushel more in Minneapolis than in Winnipeg. It needs to widen only 2 cents a bushel more to wipe out the United States duty and thus open the United States market to Canadian wheat. During the wheat-selling season, except for short periods when an exceptional occasion arises owing to a demand for wheat for lake cargoes. Minneapolis wheat prices are always higher than Winnipeg prices. It is for those who resist the demand for free wheat to Justify this state of affairs if they can.
In 1912, in the months of January, February, March, April, May, June, and July Minneapolis prices were higher than the Winnipeg prices, with the exception of one quotation. In August there were two quotations in which the Winnipeg prices were higher; in September there were three, but during the whole year only eleven out of fifty quotations were lower at Minneapolis than at Winnipeg. In 1913, in the months of January, February, and March the Minneapolis prices were all an average of two and three-quarters cents better than the Winnipeg prices. In April, May, June,

July, and August, in almost every quotation, the Winnipeg prices were a little better. In September, October, November, and December the Minneapolis prices were again better, and these were the principal selling months. This, however, brings, for the whole year, the average price to pretty much the same figure for both points. In 1914, in the months of January, February, March, April, and May the prices at Minneapolis were much better; in June there were two or three quotations in which the Winnipeg prices were higher, but altogether only sixteen out of fifty-two quotations were lower at Minneapolis than at Winnipeg. The average price, including these, was nearly two cents higher for Minneapolis. In 1915, in January, the quotations were all, except one, in favour of Minneapolis, but the difference was very slight; in February, all but two; in March, all but one; in April, all but one; in May, all but two; in June, the prices were all better at Minneapolis; in July, August, September, and October, the same; in November, all but two. In 1915, when the quotations were so nearly alike the prices were affected by war conditions, otherwise would have been much higher in Minneapolis.
I make the statement that the Winnipeg column of quotations should be headed "No. 2," and the Minneapolis column "No. 1." I am not going to read the Grain Act again, because the hon. member for As-sinaboia (Mr. Turriff) has read it already, but I will read the descriptions of Manitoba No. 2 and Minneapolis No. 1, and hon. members will see that our No. 2 is better than their No. 1, making the spread still greater.
No. 1 Northern Spring wheat shall be dry, sound, sweet, and clean, may consist of the hard and soft varieties of Spring wheat, and weigh not less than fifty-seven pounds to the measured bushel.
No. 2 Manitoba Northern wheat shall be sound and reasonably clean, of good milling qualities, and fit for warehousing, weighing not less than fifty-eight pounds to the bushel, and shall be composed of at least forty-five per cent of hard red Fife wheat.
That is, No. 1 Northern Minneapolis Spring wheat does not require to have any hard wheat in it, and it may weigh one pound less than Manitoba No. 1 Northern. There is a foot-note here in regard to Northern Spring wheat that further widens the difference, and shows the anxiety of the American millers to have Northern hard wheat. The note is as follows:
Hard, flinty wheat, of good colour, containing no appreciable admixture of soft wheat,
may be admitted into the grades of No. 2 Northern Spring wheat and No. 3 Northern Spring wheat, provided weight of the same is not more than one pound less than the minimum test weight required by the existing rules of said grades, and provided further, that such wheat is in all other respects qualified for admission into such grades.
The variety of wheat known as "Humpback," owing to its inferior milling quality, shall not be graded higher than No. 3.
The inference is very strong that the Americans cannot produce sufficient hard wheat and are consequently ready and willing to pay a good premium for the hard wheat grown in the West.
Now, I want to speak for a few minutes in regard to freight congestion. Since I have been in the West, in every year that we have a good crop there is always a great deal of congestion, suffering and loss; and it seems to me that free access to the market to the south of us would alleviate that condition of things to a very large extent, because I would imagine that the railway companies there would immediately provide in some way for transportation of our wheat to the South. At the present time our Canadian railways are not able to handle all the grain that is grown, and they should not be dogs in the manger and expect that the grain will be held at the expense of the farmers and the country generally in order that they may have the hauling of it. A good deal of the wheat, by being held in that way, would be spoiled, although, of course, as the weight would remain the same, the railway companies would get the same freight on it. As the country develops, as we hope it will do, and produces more, the railways will not be able to increase the transportation facilities in the proper proportion, and therefore it will be no detriment to them if the market to the south of us is thrown open. No doubt, however, the profits of the great milling concerns would be affected; but evidently they are making quite enough money at the present time, and I think that the Minister of Finance, under the 25 per cent clause in his Budget proposals, will find that enormous profits will have to be disgorged by the Canadian millers. They can, however, stand the loss of a certain amount of their illegitimate profits, and they will not have to pay more for their wheat than it is worth.
Although grain is put on the American market on grade, the Americans buy, not on grade, but on sample. Unfortunately I lost some statistics which I had, showing that quantities of No. 1 and No. 2 in car

lots were purchased at different prices on the same dates, thus proving that they were bought on sample. Therefore, Canadian wheat would be sold in the United States on its merits. Now, there is always a great deal of grain of inferior grades, which does not receive the price which it should receive in the Canadian market. I will just take the liberty of reading the description of one more grade, American No. 4 wheat, which is evidently a milling wheat, because it is officially graded. In the West it would not even be called chicken feed, but still the millers in the States seem to want it. The description is as follows:
No. 4 Northern Spring wheat shall include inferior spring wheat that is badly shrunken, or damaged, and weigh not less than forty-nine pounds to the measured bushel.
In our markets that wheat would not receive the price for No. 1 feed. I have raised some of that quality of wheat myself, and I have been offered 23 cents a bushel for it when good wheat was selling at 65 cents. There is no good reason why this Government should not open the market to the south of us, and they could do so easily. If the manufacturers decided that their protection should be removed, no doubt it would be done away with at once. Now, the farmers are asking, almost demanding, that their protection shall be taken away, and still it seems as if their request were not to be considered, when the only possible interest that might be affected would be the millers who are well able to take care of themselves.
Another argument advanced is that the dairymen of the East would have to pay more fox their bran and shorts. That is no argument at all;, but, even supposing it is, as flour is put on the market cheaper in Minneapolis than in Canada-according to the statistics, it is some sixty cents a barrel cheaper

it follows that bran and shorts ought to be cheaper, and in that case the dairymen of the East could obtain their bran and shorts from the United States. I do not consider that a good argument anyway. We cannot possibly get more for our wheat than it is worth, but are indebted to its full value. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) is, very properly, endeavouring to open markets throughout the world foT Canadian manufactured products. But there is a market immediately to the south of us for wheat that will open almost automatically at a word from this Government.

The opening of that market could not do harm to any interest, and there is every reason to believe that to the great bulk of our people it would be a decided advantage.
There are some Conservatives who have been impressed with the soundness of this proposal. The Toronto News of the 15th of October, 1913, said-I suppose " in a moment of weakness ":
No doubt the Western grain growers desire to have the Canadian duty removed. Probably it would be unwise to resist the demand. *	*
The grain crop of the West, however, will steadily increase, and in consideration of the action of Washington the farmers may fairly demand that the American market be opened. The Canadian mills, which manufacture chiefly for foreign markets, may not be greatly prejudiced, while possibly freight rates may be favourably affected. If the trade agreement three years ago had covered only free wheat, it is not likely that the Conservative parliamentary party would have resisted the proposal. Removal of the duty under existing conditions involves no contract with the United States, nor any limitation of the fiscal or legislative freedom of Canada.
It is most
undesirable that any legitimate appeal from the West should be rejected, or any grievance perpetuated which can be removed without endangering national interests
But
since the West clearly demands free wheat, it would probably be unwise to continue the Canadian duties which prevent free, shipments to American milling centres.
I do not know what argument can be successfully used to refute the opinions thus expressed.
I wish again to say a word on the subject of grain congestion in the West. We had a visitor here from Alberta recently, Mr. McColl, a member of the Alberta Legislature, and a large farmer. He represents the constituency of Acadia, which is on the Saskatchewan boundary and in the Goose Lake country. I understood from him that his mission was to try to arrange some way by which cars could be brought in so that the wheat could be taken out of the country. There are millions of bushels there yet unshipped. It is a magnificent country for the growing of grain of all kinds-and there has been a splendid yield this year. But the grain is still on the farmers' hands and much of it is in danger of being spoiled. The only response that Mr. McColl could get was the statement that all that was humanly possible would be done. It would be unreasonable to expect more than that. But at the same time conditions could be changed so -as to give a much greater effectiveness to that action, and there would be a great change in relieving the -situation if our wheat were admitted free into the United States. There can be no doubt that

it would have the effect of bringing into play greater facilities than we now have for the marketing of the grain. If the West is to be made productive in the way of graingrowing it is more than ever necessary that it should be possible to realize the greatest return from the crops. There is no benefit whatever in raising a lot of stuff unless you can put it on the market. It is one thing to produce and quite another thing to turn the product into money. The very object of production is to get as much money as possible. In the interest of settlement and of future grain production for the benefit of the country at large, every available market should be opened at once. To gain free entrance for our wheat into the United States certainly cannot do any harm, and we have every reason to expect that it will be of great benefit. If you are going to ask people to go to the West and to settle and become producers, you must make the country attractive to those people. There is no use in telling them merely that the country will grow all kinds of grain; you must be able to show them also that that grain can be turned into money. Many farmers have the grain to-day who are not able to turn it into money. And as time goes on this condition will grow worse, except when we have a lean year, as we sometimes do in some parts of the country.
There is no need for me to go over ground that has already been covered so ably by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), and so I conclude with the hope that the Government will take this matter into their most serious consideration and will deal with it favourably at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have listened to-day, as always,
witii close attention to the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. MacNutt). He is a man of practical judgment who puts forward his argument moderately and temperately, and is always heard with interest in this House. The - question involved in the resolution moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) is one which has on many occasions during the past few years engaged the attention of the Government. Many representations have been made, both for and against the proposal. As Minister of the department immediately concerned with tariff matters, and recognizing the importance of the question and of the discussions which have proceeded regarding it, especially in the West, I have given the subject a great deal of close personal attention. I have caused a record to be kept of prices
of grain both in Canada and in the United States, with a view to thoroughly familiarizing myself with the merits of the question in order to reach a sound and just conclusion in the national interest. When I say in the national interest, I need not say how important a factor in the national interest I consider the interest and material wellbeing of the three great grain growing provinces of the West. It is in that spirit that I have approached, from time to time, the consideration of this question.
The provisions of the Underwood Tariff, to which attention has been directed by my hon. friend from Assiniboia, are not generally understood. I do not mean to say that my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), or my hon. friend from Saltcoats (Mr. MacNutt) does not understand them.
I think they do; the wording of the resolution indicates that the hon. member for Assiniboia understands the provisions of the Underwood tariff relating to this matter, but it is a fact that the provisions of that tariff are not generally understood throughout Canada. Even my hon. friend from Assiniboia, the other evening, made what I may regard as a slip in his speech. At page 829 of Hansard he said:
Two years ago the United States put wheat on the free list to any country that adopted the same policy with regard to their wheat. All we have to do to secure the American market for the Canadian farmer is to put our wheat on the free list.
I prefer to regard that as a slip, because that is not in accordance with the facts. The Underwood tariff does not provide for the free entry of Canadian wheat to the United States upon condition of Canada admitting wheat from the United States free.
I stated in another part of my speech that wheat and wheat products and potatoes are all in the same category.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I desired to do my friend no injustice, and I stated that I did not think he was misinformed. I have quoted this to show that even he is apt to make a mis-statement about the matter, and there is a very considerable body of opinion in Canada which believes that if we admit wheat free from the United States our wheat will then automatically be permitted free into the United States. That is not the fact, and in order that we may lay a proper foundation for the discussion of this important subject, I will

place upon Hansard the provisions of the Underwood Tariff relating to it:
Item 644. Wheat, wheat flour, semolina, and other wheat products, not specially provided for: Provided, that wheat shall be subject to a duty of ten cents per bushel, that wheat flour shall be subject to a duty of forty-five cents per barrel of 196 pounds, and semolina and other products of wheat, not specially provided for, ten per centum ad valorem, when imported directly or indirectly from a country, dependency, or other subdivision of government which imposes a duty on wheat or wheat flour or semolina imported from the United States.
I desire to bring to the attention of the House, as it has a bearing on my argument and the proper discussion of this question, especially as to the matter of price, what are known as the drawback provisions of the American tariff. These provisions are to the following effect:
1.	Wheat may be shipped through the United States to other countries without payment of duty thereon;
2.	In the case of flour exported from the United States which has been manufactured in that country from imported wheat, a drawback of ninety-nine per cent of the duty upon such wheat is refunded, the American miller therefore obtaining the by-products, bran and offal, free of duty upon the wheat from which they came. In other words, the duty payable on the wheat so used is $1 per thousand bushels, or one-tenth of one cent per bushel.
3.	Upon wheat imported for consumption in the United States, the duty is ten cents per bushel.
I have given the provisions of the Underwood Tariff so far as they relate to the free entry of Canadian wheat to the United States. Their effect is, that in order to get our wheat, to say nothing of our flour or semolina into the United States, we must admit into Canada free of duty, American wheat, American flour and American semolina. The question at issue of course is: is it advantageous in the national interest and as a most important factor in that national interest, is it in the interest of the wheat growing provinces, to bring into effect the provisions of this Underwood Tariff. The deduction which I draw from the provisions of the Underwood Tariff which I have placed before the House and the drawback regulations in the American Tariff is that, so far as concerns Canadian wheat shipped through the United States or Canadian wheat manufactured in the United States into flour for export, no tariff change would materially alter the position so far as the Canadian grower or exporter of wheat is concerned. Let me repeat that: So far as concerns Canadian wheat shipped through the United States for export, or Canadian wheat manu-

fatcured in the United States into flour for export, no tariff change would materially alter the position so far as the Canadian grower or exporter of wheat is concerned. The question can only arise in the case of wheat imported into the United States for consumption there. It is contended by those who favour this legislation that the Canadian farmer would obtain the benefit of the higher prices prevailing at Minneapolis. I have pointed out that the change would only be necessary if it should be considered advisable to supply the home market of the United States, because of the drawback provisions which I have mentioned. Today the American miller at Minneapolis can buy Canadian wheat and pay the duty of ten cents per bushel upon it; he can grind it into flour and he can export it from the United States and get a drawback of ninety-nine per cent of the ten cents per bushel duty which he has paid. So, as I have stated, the question narrows itself down to this: Is it in the interest of the Canadian farmer and of Canada, that our wheat should find its way to the great milling centres of the United States, to be ground into flour there for home consumption.
I desire to point out in this connection that the United States has a continually increasing surplus of export wheat, which is exported either in the form of grain or flour. The surplus wheat for export in the United States from the last crop is no less than 390,000,000 bushels. The exportable surplus from Canada will be 264,000,000 bushels; so that the situation on the face of it, although! I do not put this forward as a conclusive argument, but subject to qualification, that the United States presumably has not only -sufficient wheat for its own domestic requirements, but sufficient to enable it to export, either in the form of wheat or of flour, 390,000,000 bushels, while Canada has a surplus of 264,000,000 bushels, which -she can export -in the form of wheat or of flour.
The outstanding fact, therefore, with regard to -the two nations in respect of their production of wheat, is that they aTe in competition in the wheat and flour markets of the world. Canada and the United States are two of the keenest competitors in the export markets of the world for th-eir surplus production of wheat, either in the form of the grain itself, or of flour. It is not as if the United States consumes all her wheat; -she has this large exportable surplus. It was pointed out by the hon.

gentleman (Mr.. MacNutt) and by the hon. member for Assiniboia, that there is at times a substantial spread dn favour of Minneapolis and Du'luth as against Winnipeg and Fort William. I think these are the proper points of comparison because, as they contend, the price is higher at Minneapolis than it is at Winnipeg, or higher at Duluth than it is at Fort William, my hon. friends assume that if the existing tariff were changed the Canadian farmer would be able to get the higher price prevailing at Minneapolis. I desire to point out the fallacy that underlies the argument of the hon. gentleman (Mr. MacNutt) and it is this: he has placed upon Hansard figures which show a spread at times under the existing tariff situation, and he has not, and of course could not, place figures upon Hansard showing what would be the result, in regard to the prices at Minneapolis and Duluth, if the present tariff situation were changed. I purpose developing that argument a little later.
One would think, Mr. Speaker, that as the United States has an exportable surplus, and that Canada has an exportable surplus, the export price would govern; and yet it is a fact that at times-and it is alleged, although I do not concede it, that more frequently at Minneapolis than at Winnipeg-the price is in favour of the American market. I need not tell the House, because this question has been up for discussion on many previous occasions, that the reason for the higher price which prevails at Minneapolis in the fall, and sometimes at other periods, is that Minneapolis is a great milling centre, and that the milling industry requires hard wheat to grind with the softer varieties from the southern and western States for the purpose of making flour. In other words, a local demand exists at Minneapolis which is, in a measure, independent of the export price. That is the substantial outstanding fact with regard to the Minneapolis price of wheat; that it is dependent upon a local demand which is, as I have stated, in a measure independent of the export price. There is truth in the statement that the Minneapolis price is higher than the Canadian price. Since last September I have caused statistics to be gathered, and the spread in price has been from three to eight cents a bushel, or even more, in favour of the American market. A little later, I shall mention some exceptional features of the economic situation of the past year which would account, or tend
to account, for the continuation of that spread. There is some truth in the statement, but as they say in the law courts, *it is not the truth, tiie whole truth, and nothing but the truth. It is that we desire to get at.
I intend to maintain that the supposed advantage which the Canadian farmer is being led to believe he would obtain at Minneapolis, is largely, -if not wholly, illusory. That is to say, I contend that if the tariff were taken off by the United States to-day, the price of wheat at Minneapolis would fall to the export price, or very close to it. Personally, I believe it would fall to the export price.
Mr. MkcNUTT: There is some room for it to fall.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would fall, and my hon. friend knows that the greater distance you fall the greater the drop and the greater the shock.
Mr. MaoNUTT: It could not fall lower than it is at Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would not fall lower than the Winnipeg export price, but it would fall to the Winnipeg export price, or very close to it. I believe it would fall to the Winnipeg export price, because the export price would govern. Freights are precisely the same from the United States to the great market of the world in Liverpool as they aTe from Winnipeg or Fort William. The freights are equalized, and therefore I maintain that the export price would govern. In that connection I desire to read an extract from the Wall Street Journal, which is a very reputable and well known financial organ in the United States. The extract was copied in the Montreal Gazette of November 8, 1915, and I quote it simply to show the point of view of that Journal. The article reads:
The Canadian farmer believes he would get at least five cents more for his wheat were he free to ship direct to Minneapolis. He does not stop to think that were the American markets free to him and he chucked 200,000,000 bushels of Canadian wheat on the American markets in the first three months of the harvest, the price of wheat in America would utterly collapse. The American millers and the American railroads, as well as American bankers and merchants naturally desire to see all Canadian grain marketed through Chicago and Minneapolis.
But such a process would most certainly demoralize prices, and both the Canadian and American farmers would get lower prices for their grain. Were all duties on grain and flour eliminated from the tariffs of the United States and Canada the millers would be the

chief beneficiaries. The American millers would draw on the Canadian prairies for the brands of wheat they lack for mixing purposes, and the Canadian millers would buy cheaper than they are getting.
I put that forward, not as endorsing it, but simply as the view of a reputable financial journal in the United States. I put forward, also, not as endorsing it, but as a western view, an article from the Regina Evening Province of January 15.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I put it forward as showing a western point of view, because what we are really arguing is the question, not so much of the spread that exists between Minneapolis and Winnipeg, but whether or not a spread would exist if the tariff wall were down. This extract from the Regina Province is:
If a favourable result on this resolution

he is speaking of the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff).
-resulted, does any one doubt what the effect would be? On a mere rumour that Canada intended to remove the duty on wheat, last fall, the price of wheat In Chicago broke sharply, going several points downward, and it did not recover until the free wheat rumour was discredited. If free wheat were actually put in force the result would be to lower immediately the price the Canadian farmer is now getting for his wheat at Winnipeg.
-I have been trying to deal with this matter fairly and judicially, and I think there is a very great deal of merit in the argument put forward in these articles, and for this reason: Tbe price of an article depends upon supply and demand. If there is more than enough wheat to supply the local demand what will happen to the price of wheat? The price of wheat will fall. I am dealing with this question on general business principles, and i it is inconceivable to me that, if the American tariff were down, and there was ready to descend upon Minneapolis a tide of hard wheat from our prairie provinces, the price of wheat at Minneapolis would not fall. It must fall.
Under such circumstances would it not necessarily follow that the millers of Canada would not have to pay any more than they now have to nay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not yet dealt with the milling question; I will come to it in due course, and I hope to be able to deal with it to the satisfaction of my hon. friend. The question of free wheat did not arise actually last year. Why did it not arise last year? Because, as a mat-
[Sir Thomas White.!
ter of fact, the Canadian price for wheat during last year was very much better than the American price. Let me place upon Hansard a memorandum prepared by my office, where, as I have stated, a careful record is kept of the comparative prices of wheat.
