speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I read what the hon. gentleman said the other day as to that, and while attaching some weight to it, at the same time the figures which I have given here afford a fair basis of comparison. I may say to my hon. friend further that, allowing his argument, there is enough margin to spare in the difference of five cents between Winnipeg and Minneapolis in favour of Winnipeg, and two and three-fifths cents in favour of Fort William as against Duluth.
In these days we would not sell in Minneapolis; we would sell at home.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have handed to me a chart prepared by Mr. Sanford Evans as to quotations of grain prices, and I propose to lay it on the table of the House.
1 think any hon. gentleman will find this chart interesting. It shows the variations and fluctuations in the prices of grain on both sides of the line. Sometimes the price is higher on one side and sometimes on the other, but this is to be said, and it is a point to which I intend to revert later, that when Canadian wheat is being pressed forward for sale .the tendency is for the Canadian price to be lower than the American.
What period does that chart cover?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
1912-13-14-15. It is said that the price is more frequently higher at Minneapolis, but, as I say, that begs the question. The real question is not whether the price is higher at Minneapolis under existing tariff conditions, but the question is: what would be the state of affairs if the present tariff situation were changed?
I desire to again emphasize that the Underwood tariff does not provide for the free entry of wheat in exchange for free wheat, but the Underwood tariff provides for the free entry of three products in exchange for the free entry of three products. I now proceed to deal with that aspect of the question. Why did not the Underwood tariff, as in the case of potatoes, provide for free wheat in exchange for free wheat? What object had the framers of the American tariff in view when they provided, not for the free entry of wheat from countries
which afforded free entry of American wheat, but provided that three products should be admitted to that country in return for the admission of the same three products from another country? It is perfectly obvious that the framers of the Underwood tariff desired to gain for their flour free access to markets of the countries whose wheat was admitted free.
I do not blame the framers of the Underwood tariff for that; I think it was wise from their standpoint to make that provision when dealing with the question. In substance, what they say to Canada is this: If we allow your wheat to come in free, we want to grind it, and sell it back to you in the form of flour. That, in a word, is the idea that the framers of the Underwood tariff had in mind when these provisions were enacted. I am not finding any fault with that policy; it was for them to determine what the provisions of their tariff should be. The framing of a tariff is essentially a domestic matter, and each country has to provide as seems best to its legislators in the interests of the country which they represent. It is to be pointed out that the United States is one of the great milling countries of the world. The United States has 7,500 mills, with a daily capacity of just about 1,000,000 barrels. Minneapolis alone, the great centre that I have been speaking of, has a daily capacity of 73,800 barrels, representing a consumption of 330,000 bushles of wheat. The object of the Underwood tariff was to secure a great export business for the American flour merchant. Now, what about the capacity of Canada. Canada is a great flour milling country too. The flour milling industry in Canada has been encouraged by all Governments, and just here I should like to point out that when my right hon. friend's Government framed the provisions of the reciprocity agreement they insisted that there should be a protection of fifty cents a barrel on Canadian flour; so do not let it be said that the Government of my right hon. friend, when in power, overlooked the question of protection to the Canadian miller. The flour milling capacity of Canada is as follows: Canada has 550 mills, with a capacity of 100,000 barrels per day, or one-tenth of the flour capacity of the United States mills. I have given the flour milling capacity of the United States and of Canada, and it is to be pointed out that if we bring into effect the provisions of the Underwood tariff the Canadian milling industry will at once come into compe-



tition with the highly specialized flour milling industry of the United States, which, holding its own home market, would at the same time seriously injure the Canadian milling industry.
Now, I do not contend that if it appeared to be clearly in the national interests that one industry should be hampered or crippled, that that should not be done; but I do say that before any such action should be taken it should appear to be clearly in the national interests, and in the interests of those who think they would be advantaged by the legislation in question. I contend that the advantage should be sufficiently wide to constitute a national advantage, and further, that it should have the element of a permanent advantage before .any steps should be taken which would have the effect of crippling or even destroying a great Canadian industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not the figures, but one of my colleagues informs me that the export business is comparatively small. .The figures are very easily obtainable. Let us assume foT a moment that the position taken by my hon. friend from Assiniboia is correct.
It is quite correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Sometimes we make very far-fetched assumptions in this House. Let us assume that he is correct in supposing that our wheat would flow down to Minneapolis if the duty was removed. It is obvious that if our grain did flow down to Minneapolis it. would not remain in Canada to be ground by our mills, nor would it be carried from Canada by our transportation systems to the markets of the world. If free wheat will be a real, and not an illusory, advantage to the farmers of the West, that is what would happen. My hon. friend put forward the argument, with a great deal of force I must say, that the Canadian millers would not be injured because they would have open to them the American market. Now, in that connection it is to be pointed out that it takes a very considerable time for any industry to establish itself and develop in a foreign country. The question of brands, for instance, is one of great importance. In order to develop their business in the United States, the Canadian millers would have to spend large sums of money in the

United States, and they would have to dc that-and I desire to emphasize this point as strongly as I can-in the face of the utmost uncertainty as to the continuance of the provisions of the .Underwood tariff. My hon. friend from Assiniboia said that the farmers of the Northwest States were restive with regard to this question, and did not like i the idea of Canadian wheat being admitted. Is there any certainty as to these provisions of the Underwood tariff? How far will business interests be justified in spending hundreds of thousands of dollars for the purpose of developing their trade in a foreign country, if they are confronted with a possibility, or a strong probability to the minds of many of them, that tariff changes may be put into effect in the not far distant future which will shut them out from that market? I desire to say again that I do not contend that if the change appeared clearly in the national interest, and in estimating that national interest the interest and welfare of three great provinces have to be taken into consideration-the interest of one industry should be determinative. If it was perfectly clear to me that it was in the interest of the country that the milling interest should take its chances, I know the view that I would take; but it is not clear to me and it is not clear to any member of this House that, with the tariff down, there would be any substantial advantage to the Canadian grain grower to have the Minneapolis market. It is not clear that there is any element of permanence in the provisions of the Underwood tariff which we have now under consideration, and therefore from the milling standpoint and from the standpoint of the grain growers themselves, it fwould seem to me that we should be very sure of our ground before we take a step which may have irrevocable consequences.
Now, I have dealt with the matter from the standpoint of the milling industry, but there are other standpoints. This country has a great mixed farming industry and I suppose that in no part of Canada has the mixed farming industry made greater strides in the past few years than in the western provinces. I stated the other day, and I state now, that I always assume that farmers know the class of farming which it is best for them to carry on, having regard to all the conditions. Suppose a homesteader takes up land in the Northwest; it is all very well to talk about his going into mixed farming, but the immediate problem that presents itself to him is how he can

get a crop in and get a profit from it. Having regard to the conditions with which homesteaders and settlers generally are confronted, I say it is reasonable to assume that they know the class of farming which it is best for them to engage in.
And the class of markets too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Therefore, as I
stated the other day, I have never written essays nor delivered lectures as to the class of fanning which should be carried on by the intelligent farmers of this country or of any part of it, and I do not propose, to do so. I am going to be pragmatical and assume that the farmers in any particular section of this country know what is best for them so far as the carrying on of farming is concerned, in the section in which they are engaged in agriculture and under the conditions in which they find themselves. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) speaks of markets. This question has been made a political question, but if it wrere discussed dispassionately by hon. gentlemen opposite, and if the farmers were told the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, I do not believe that the farmers of the West, en masse, or in any large majority, or in a majority, would be desirous of seeking the illusory market at Minneapolis. This is more a political question than an economic question to-day. My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), on page 829 of Hansard, made a rather extraordinary statement with regard to the export price obtained by the Canadian farmer. These are his words:
But what do we find when the wheat got to Liverpool? Instead of the Manitoba farmer getting seven or eight cents less a bushel than the American farmer, he received from the Liverpool merchant from six to eight cents a bushel more than the American farmer, and that cannot be denied by any one who knows anything about the grain trade.

If the hon. minister will allow me, I was not correctly reported there, and I changed that portion of my speech when I got the copy of Hansard. I did not say those words at all, nor say words that meant anything like that. What I said was, that while the Canadian wheat was seven or eight sents a bushel lower, when that wheat got to Liverpool, it sold for seven or eight cents higher than the corresponding Minneapolis grade.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Now let us see what follows from that. The Canadian
wheat brings more at Liverpool. The transportation charges are precisely the same. Who gets the six cents or eight cents?
That is for the Government to explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All right. Who buys the grain from the farmer in the Northwest? Who is the greatest grain buyer in the Northwest? The Grain Growers' Grain Association. I ask my hon. friend to go to the source of authoritative information in this matter, and ask the Grain Growers' Grain Association why it is that his statement is correct, as he states it is correct, and when he has explained that to the farmers of the West, let him come down and give us also the benefit of the explanation.
I do not think the Grain Growers' Grain Association export any wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But they buy it.
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, that is the point I am making. I am told by the Solicitor General that they are great exporters.
I would not rely on the Solicitor General's experience in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from Assiniboia has got himself into a dilemma from which he cannot extricate himself.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He says that
Canadian wheat sells in Liverpool at from six cents to eight cents more a bushel, and that charges are equal. Well, who gets the difference? The buyers. And who are the buyers? The principal buyers are the Grain Growers' Grain Company. One useful result of this discussion may be that my hon. friend who, I have no doubt,' will say he approaches this question conscientiously and judicially, will interest himself in finding out why the Grain Growers' Grain Company does not pay more.
I can tell the hon. minister that I took the very information I gave to the House from the Grain Growers' Guide.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not doubt it. I do not blame my hon. friend for taking

information from the Grain Growers' Guide, but I cannot help expressing surprise that he should be so unsophisticated as to put it forward here as a conclusive argument in favour of bringing our tariff into conformity with the Underwood tariff. If my hon. friend got that information from the Grain Growers' Guide, I think he had better ask the Grain Growers' Guide for an explanation of it. He made another observation :
But during September, October and November, the farmers of the West lost over $10,000,000 in not being able to have the American market for their wheat.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend, as we used to say in the old school days, is begging the question.
I never do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think he is begging the question. He finds a quotation of wheat in Minneapolis, and at once assumes that if the tariff were down our farmers could get that quotation. But if the tariff were down, the quotation would drop with the tariff, and instead of the farmers gaining 'ten million dollars the only effect would be that the price in Minneapolis would be equalized with the price in Winnipeg. The hon. gentleman proceeds :
The Government would not give them ,the American market, they sent their wheat to the old country, and the farmer is paying from 40 cents to 45 cents a bushel to take his wheat from tide water to Liverpool.
Just to show the unfairness-I will say the unintentional unfairness of the hon.
gentleman-
Do not be so particular.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will take him at
his word then, and say, just to show his unfairness, I will quote a little further:
For ' the munition manufacturers who were able to charge this and the~British Government four prices for their goods, they could get a rate which was practically the same as the rate before the war, but the rate for carrying wheat which, before the' war, was from 5 to 7 cents a bushel, went up to from 40 to 45 cents a bushel. The Government were either powerless or careless, or they did not have the interest of the farmers at heart to the same degree that they had the interest of the manufacturers, they did not give them the American market and they allowed them to be robbed on this last year's crob to the extent of $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 in excessive freight rates.
Now, my hon. friend has a conscience, and how he could cause a statement like that to

be put on the wire to be sent to the people of the West, I cannot understand. I think he underrates the intelligence of his constituents and of the people of the West generally if he thinks that they will believe any such statement. It is true that freight rates on wheat have been seven or eight times what they were. But I can tell the hon. member, as a matter of economics, that the *Canadian farmer does not pay those freights. If the freights could be put down to normal, the price would drop in Liverpool. He takes the freights from Canada or New York. But consider also the freights from Argentina and Australia. If we consider the whole situation, there is no conclusion possible except that the consumer in Great Britain pays, almost in entirety, the increase in the freight rates.
Now, I have dealt with this question from the standpoint of the farmer of the plains, and I have dealt with it from the standpoint of the milling industry; I now propose to deal with it from the standpoint of general Canadian policy. There is no man. in this House who does not know the policy that has ruled in this country. That policy is this: that as far as practicable Canadian raw material should be manufactured in Canada, transported over our railway systems, and sent out through Canadian ports to the markets of the world. That has been the national policy of the Conservatives, and, despite what may be said to the contrary, it has also been the policy of the Liberals. That policy has been followed with the object of building up our industries. I said a moment ago that we weTe charged with being solicitous about the millers. I do not think I was very solicitous about them yesterday. I think we should be regardful of all great interests. Even in the *reciprocity pact of the late Government of which my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) was a distinguished and important supporter, the Government were so solicitous-would my hon. friend say over-solicitous?-about the millers, that, in order to protect their interests, they insisted on a duty of 50 cents a barrel.
That is what defeated us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can tell my hon. friend what among other things, defeated them. For one thing there was no advantage to the Canadian producers in the pact And for another thing, there was the fact, of the pact itself, the fact that it was an agreement, an interlocking of our tariff with the tariff of the country to the south. I

have been an attentive listener to debates in this House ever since I had the honour of becoming a member, and I believe I have heard this theme of manufacturing within Canadian boundaries, transportation over Canadian rail and water routes, and the development of Canadian harbours, for the export of our goods to the markets of the world more frequently discussed than any other subject. Let the question of transportation come up and what aTe the Maritime Provinces interested in? Ports. Our canal system is one of our most frequent subjects of discussion. Money has been poured out by hundreds of millions of dollars to develop our transcontinental railway systems. No subject has been discussed so extensively in this House as this of manufacturing our own raw material, building our own transportation systems, and improving our harbours for extension of our trade to the markets of the world. Now, I ask this House, is that a sound national policy, or is it not? I do not believe that any member of this House dare rise in his constituency and say that we should reverse this policy, which has been followed by all governments in this country practically since Confederation, or, at all events since 1879. This involves a departure from that'policy which has been followed by all governments and which has commended itself to the people of this country. I made it plain in my Budget speech of 1914 that if it were clearly in the national interest that that policy should be departed from in some respect, I would not say it would not be the duty of the Government to depart from it. I would he disposed to say that would be the duty of the Government, because national policy is based upon national interest; and if it was clearly in the national interest to change any part of it, why, of /course, the Government would be wise in making the change. But I contend that the advantage must be clear and unmistakable. If it is contended that an advantage will be gained from the American market for Canadian wheat secured through our adopting a policy which involves-a departure from the principles which have governed the Conservative Governments of the past and the Liberal Government of the past, I say that the advantage should be clear, that it should be substantial, and that it should have a character of permanence. I have, shown that it is clear that this is going to be of no substantial advantage to the grain growers. I have stated that the supposed advantage is largely illusory, and
I think I have proved it. At all events, it is not substantial. My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) admitted the other night that the prices would equalize, that the Canadian growers would not get the whole advantage of the Minneapolis price, but only a part. I think they will get such a small part, if any, that the advantage would not be substantial. At all events it is not clear to me that it would be substantial.
Now, what about permanence? Is there any man in this House who can say that the provisions of the Underwood tariff will be in operation two years from now? Whether we change our tariff under the terms of this resolution or not, a tariff is a domestic matter. The Underwood tariff makes an offer which can be accepted by the Canadian Government in its tariff, but there is nothing to hinder the American Government, this fall or a year from this fall, from radically changing its tariff in this regard and rescinding the provisions of the Underwood tariff to which I have referred. Therefore I contend that the supposed advantage is not clear, that it is not substantial, and that it has not the character of permanence. I say that all those three elements should be present, and present unmistakably, before we should depart from what has been regarded by the people of this country as a sound, national policy. Is there a man in this House who believes that with a production of hard wheat such as we have in our Northwest, increasing from year to year, that if the tariff were taken down and a tide of fifty or one hundred or one hundred and fifty or two hundred million bushels of wheat was ready to descend on Minneapolis, the price would not break? Every one of us knows that the price would break.
There are other aspects of this matter which I touched upon in the Budget speech. I summed up the arguments pro and con. In connection with the discussion of this subject and the agitation for the change in our tariff which would bring into effect the provisions of the Underwood tariff, I have received from certain railway employees a petition urging that their interests would be very seriously affected, that if the wheat went south-and the assumption of my hon. friend is that the wheat will go south or else there is no point in his argument-serious injury would be done to them. 1 do not say that any of these grounds that are put forward against this proposal are

conclusive; I have only put them forward to show the doubt which exists as to the result which would accrue from taking this very radical step and changing this policy which has been in the past regarded as national.
Then we have had petitions from mixed farmers. The mixed farmers say that bran and offal are more expensive in the United States than here and that consequently, if this went into effect, both in the Northwest and Ontario the farmer would have to pay more for his bran and offal. It is put forward also that if we took the step contemplated by this resolution the milling industry would certainly not be extended into the Northwest. I have given that matter as careful consideration as I think I ever gave a question in my life, and I have come to the conclusion that if this were done the Canadian milling industry would not be extended further into the Northwest for this reason, that the markets lie to the [DOT] east and south and while the milling would be done in Canada east of Winnipeg, to the extent that our millers might he able to carry it on with American competition, there is no likelihood, so far as we can judge at present, of an extension to the Canadian Northwest of the milling industry. I need not tell hon. members that upon the milling industry mixed farming largely depends for its well being. The offal, the bran which the farmers use for the rearing of their livestock, is of supreme importance to the farming community and this proposed change would have an important bearing upon the supply of bran and offal for the rearing of stock by those engaged in the mixed farming industry. .1 think the small miller would probably disappear and that the business of the large millers would be very seriously affected if not crippled, and that the extension of the milling industry in the Northwest would be prevented.
I have pointed out that in the year preceding this last year's crop, 1914-15, the prices were better at Winnipeg and Fort William than at Minneapolis and Duluth. Now we come to this year. This year has been an extraordinary year. In the first place, we have been engaged in a very terrible war. Ocean transport has been interfered with as never before in the lifetime of any one in this Chamber. All the conditions have been abnormal, and to add to the abnormal conditions brought about by the war, we had the further condition that rains set in in certain parts of the

United States and that wheat which was expected to be marketed at a certain date was not available for market until a later date. What resulted from that? There resulted speculation in the great American grain centres. The Canadian farmer might well contend, if he believed, as my hon. friend does, that this would be an advantage to him, that he does not care if there is speculation or not so long as he gets his price. I think that is a proper position for him to take. But I am pointing out that this is an exceptional, an unusual, an abnormal year, and that consequently this is not a year upon the record of which we should take a step involving so radical a departure from the policy which has been followed in the past by both Liberal and Conservative Governments.
There was another feature this year: It was expected that the Dardanelles would be opened and Russian wheat released. Hon. gentlemen know that that was expected for a very considerable time and this expectation had an important bearing on the price of wheat; it tended to facilitate the speculation in the large grain centres of the United States. Another feature I think is well worthy of the consideration of this House, with a view to seeing if there is any way in which it could be overcome, and it is a problem to which I have given a good deal of thought and intend to give a good deal more.	-
If it could be overcome, I think conditions would be much better for the farmer in the western provinces; that is, that the grain movement is hurried too much. I have no faulty to find with that situation. I assume that if a man rushes his grain to market it is his own business; he is the judge. But as a matter of fact it is when our grain is hurried to the market in immense quantities that this disparity exists in a larger degree between the markets in our country and the markets of the United States. It is when we have a big load that the Canadian grain usually stands lower than the American grain. That statement may not be quite accurate, but I think it' is sufficiently accurate for the purpose.
Great Britain purchases grain as she needs it. She does not purchase in advance, and consequently, if you have immense quantities of grain seeking a market, and grain being purchased in Liverpool or the other grain centres of Great Britain, or of Europe, as required, you have of course an excess supply and a limited demand, and consequently a fall in price. I desire

to put on record here the remarks which I made in my Budget speech of 1914 with regard to this subject. In that speech I summarized, the arguments, both pro and con, as fairly as I could, and at' the conclusion of my remarks I indicated the position of the Government upon the subject of free wheat so called. After putting forward the arguments which I have advanced here to-day, and, I think, all the arguments put forward on the other side by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) and the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. MacNutt); after pointing out that we were engaged in the construction of transcontinental systems of railway, of the Hudson Bay railway, and in the development of our ports; that the Panama canal was about to be opened, and that we might expect that Vancouver would be an outlet for Canadian wheat going by the Panama canal to the markets of the world, I made these observations:
Haying regard to all these considerations, we have been unable, after having given the question most painstaking attention, to bring ourselves to the view that so great a change, involving by possibility such serious consequences, should be favourably considered until at least we are more certain as to the outcome of our vast railway development and the result to the western grain grower of the opening of the competitive routes which will be afforded by the Hudson Bay Railway and the Panama Canal. It is surely the part of wisdom to await the outcome of the developments rather than to take a step now which might involve the risk of grave and irreparable injury to our milling industry and by consequence to our live stock industry and to our transportation systems through the diversion of traffic to routes other than Canadian,
That was the attitude of the Government at that time upon the arguments and considerations put forward on this question in the discussion of this resolution.
There is a further consideration which I regard as of supreme consequence. We are in the midst of the greatest war, as has been said, of all history, and we are part of an Empire which, I believe, is sustaining the largest burden of that war. A national debt is being piled up by Great Britain to an amount which a few years ago would have staggered the imagination of the financiers and statesmen of the world. We are in the midst of this war. Are we half way through? How much further have we to go? What will be the debt of the United Kingdom when this war is concluded, as we hope and pray, in a lasting peace? What will be the fiscal burdens of the United Kingdom? How will these fiscal burdens be met? Will the same system that has
prevailed, continue to prevail, or will the statesmen of the United Kingdom, and possibly the statesmen of the Empire, have to sit down altogether, either alone or with Allies, and consider what is the wisest fiscal policy to adopt to meet the altered situation. Will that have to be done? So far as I can see, it is expected that it will be done; it is inevitable, it must be done. I do not pretend to say-he would be a presumptions man who would guess-what the fiscal policy of the United Kingdom will be after this war, but I feel perfectly satisfied in my own mind that it will not he the fiscal policy that prevailed before the war.
'That will be sad for England. '

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it will be sad
for England, I have no doubt the wisdom of British statesmen, if they agree with my right hon. friend, will find some other way. But I am expressing my own view, and I have great respect for the view of my right hon. friend, when I say that, having regard to the obligations that are being incurred by the United Kingdom, that will be incurred, and must be incurred before this war is concluded, I do not believe that the same fiscal policy can prevail in the United Kingdom as prevailed before the outbreak of this war. I do not believe further although I do not desire to interfere in the domestic affairs of even the Mother Country -that the policy which has been adopted is the wisest policy for a nation which has as powerful enemies as Great Britain has had during the last few years.
Does that include Mr. Runciman?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
can include him if he desires; I do not know to what he refers. What is to be the fiscal policy of Great Britain and the Empire? I do not know, but I would hope that the question of a preference within the British Empire is not a dead question. I would hope that it is a live question, that it'will be a live question. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is, I think, on common ground with me here, because it is only a few years ago since he desired a preference in the British market; so that unless he has changed his views since, and even if he has changed them, he is not likely to admit it in this House, , we are practically at one in the desire that there should be a preference within the British Empire. The Empire will nave to cuddle up after the war is over. What is the point I am making? Suppose that we bring into effect the provisions of

the Underwood tariff, is a preference possible without going back to the position which we now occupy? History is sometimes interesting and I want to place upon the record of this House, because it may be useful, if not in this debate, in some other, and it is sufficiently pertinent, a matter of historical interest which has a direct bearing upon the question of preference. I have in my hand the copy of:
"An Act for reducing the duty on wheat and Wheat flour, the produce of the province of Canada, imported thence into the United Kingdom" (6 & 7 Vic., cap. XXIX, 12th July, 1843).
And I am going to read the recital in order that the House may see my point:
"Whereas on the Twelfth Day of October One thousand eight hundred and forty-two an Act was passed by the Legislative Council and Legislative Assembly of the province of Canada, and reserved by the Governor General for the signification of Her Majesty's pleasure imposing a duty of three shillings sterling money of Great Britain on each imperial quarter of wheat imported into Canada, except from the United Kingdom or any of Her Majesty's Possessions, and being the growth and produce thereof: And whereas it is recited in the said Act that it was passed in the confident belief and expectation that upon the imposition of a duty upon foreign wheat imported in the province Her Majesty would be graciously pleased to recommend to Parliament the removal or reduction of the duties on wheat and wheat flour imported into the said United Kingdom from Canada: And whereas, in consideration of the duty so imposed by the said Act of the Legislature of Canada it is expedient that, if Her Majesty shall be pleased to give Her Sanction to the said Act, the duties imposed by an Act made and passed in the last session of Parliament, intituled "An Act to amend the Laws for the Importation of Corn', upon wheat and wheat flour, the produce of and imported from the province of Canada, entered for Home Consumption in the United Kingdom, should be reduced as hereinafter is mentioned:"
In other words, Great Britain was about *to give a preference to her colony, Canada and, what was the condition precedent? It was that Canada should adopt a duty as against com-the generic term for grain -imported from any other country except the Uniited Kingdom. Why? Canada could not get a preference in the British market for her wheat if wheat from a foreign country could find its way into Canada without paying duty and could be exported as Canadian wheat.
While I am on that point, let me refer for a moment to a matter -(hat I overlooked. It is conceded that if we adopted the principle of this resolution, and acted upon it, our grain would be mixed with the inferior grain of the United States and would lose its identity. My hon. friend from Assini-

boia said himself that our grain is worth six to eight cents a bushel more in Liverpool and how he can come to the conclusion that this change is in the interest of Canada, admitting that onr grain is worth six to eight cents more in Liverpool, if it involves the mingling of our wheat with American wheat, the de-grading of our wheat and the loss of its identity, passes my comprehension. Then this measure goes on and enacts the necessary legislation to carry into effect the idea embodied in the preamble. I have here also the Canadian Act-

Why not the Lord's
Prayer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, the Lord's Prayer is always in order and sometimes I have thought it would do my hon. friend good if it were said in this Chamber, especially that part of it in which we pray to be delivered from evil.
And lead us not into temptation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have here the Canadian Act in which it is recited that:
And whereas the introduction of foreign wheat, into the United Kingdom free of duty, after the introduction of the same into Canada free of duty, would be in manifest violation of the said intention of the laws of the said United Kingdom; And whereas the chief objection to the free admission of wheat and wheat flour into the said United Kingdom from Canada, arises from the free admission of foreign wheat into Canada-
I will put these recitals upon Hansard.
What is the date of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is before my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) was born, and when a wiser generation lived. The result was that they got a preference.
Does my hon. friend remember that there was a movement for annexation in Canada at that time after the repeal of that preference by Great Britain, and that reciprocity which followed cured the evil.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let me ask my hon. friend another question-I want to teach him some of the history of those early times: What happened in 1S(T>
when reciprocity came to an end? Canadian trade with the United States had been developed under the Reciprocity Treaty, and the United States abrogated that treaty in 1865-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: 1865 or 1866; let us say 1866-we will not quarrel about a year. In 1866 the treaty was abrogated, and what happened? As a matter of fact we all know what happened. It took about ten or twelve years before the country got on its feet, and when it got on its feet the people said: We are going to have a Canadian policy, the result of which is Canada as it is to-day. If my hon. friend wants to exchange views on history, I am quite prepared to meet him on his own ground. There is another feature of this question, and then I am done.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, I know our friends are tired, but they have often tired me, and as they believe in reciprocity they should not complain. There is another feature of this matter, not to be set up against the clear national interest, if it is clear, but important in the consideration of the question. I do not believe it is a wise fiscal policy to fit your tariff into the notches of another country's tariff, because any action on their part relating to a matter in which your tariff interlocks with theirs causes you to change your tariff. In other words, you react to their action, and if you have not the element of certainty then you had better have your tariff stand on its own basis. Even if you have the element of certainty, it does not follow that you should enter into a tariff agreement unless you are sure that your doing so is in the interest of the country.
What may be the result of this change if we founded our autonomy upon it? To be effectual the grain would go south, with the interruption of our present economic system and with no certainty of permanency. I think this is one of the most important factors in the consideration of this question.
I have dealt With wheat, and my hon. friend from Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes) is anxious about the potato question. I think there must be some Irish in him, but he wants to know about potatoes. The Underwood Tariff provides that potatoes shall be free.
Provided, that any of the foregoing specified articles shall be subject to a duty of 10 per centum ad valorem when imported directly or indirectly from a country, dependency, or other subdivision of government which imposes a duty on such articles imported from the United States.
I do not believe there has ever been a better market for our potatoes than exists in the home market of Canada to-day.
That is on account of the crop shortage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Crop failures
are not confined to any one portion of the hemisphere. Let me ask my hon. friend a question. If the Canadian prices were lower than the United States prices would the crop shortage prevent him from putting forward the figures? I know how strongly he would argue that, crop failures or no crop failure, we ought to take advantage of the Underwood tariff provision. So it works both ways. I desire to give some figures on the potato. It is a homely subject, but the potato is an honoured vegetable, and we might spend a worse five minutes than in considering the tariff with regard to it. The 'Canadian prices are taken from the Labour Gazette, an organ that I know will command the confidence of the former Postmaster General, and the American figures from the Monthly Crop Report of the Department of Agriculture, Washington::
