My hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes), who wants our potatoes admitted free to the United States in exchange for free entry of their potatoes to

us, will observe that the price at Sydney, Halifax and St. John in 1915 was $1, whereas the highest price in the same year in the United States was 95 cents, and the average only 61-6 cents. First, then, because it is not clear that there will be any advantage, and secondly, because if there will be any advantage it will be but a very minor advantage, and thirdly, because there is no element of permanence in an arrangement such as is contemplated in the resolution of my hon. friend, and because it involves a departure from the established national policy of this country, a policy which has been followed by all Governments in the past, and because we are in the midst .of a war and its abnormal conditions, and further because of the possibility of a fiscal arrangement not only of the tariff policy' of Great Britain, but of the tariffs of the Empire-on these grounds my view is that this resolution should be negatived.
Mr. MARCH,: We in eastern Canada are most interested in the price of flour. Can the minister tell us how it is that the price of flour is continually on the increase notwithstanding the increased competition in the West, increased railway facilities, and all the advantages of the national policy which have been so eloquently dilated upon by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Prime Minister tells me that there has been laid on the Table this afternoon the report of the High Cost of Living Commission, which deals with the subject my hon. friend refers to.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the whole western country, if not the whole agricultural population of the Dominion, will feel a very keen sense of disappointment when they learn of the remarks of the Finance Minister. The more so, because by reason of his remarks on the Budget yesterday, they had every hope that a new era had opened, in which a new line of policy would be pursued by the Government by reason of those very conditions upon which my hon. friend has laid such stress in the speech he has just made. The Minister of Finance in his speech yesterday said':
The future of Canada rests with the development of its great resources, of which the greatest and most fundamental is agriculture, and this development is in turn bound up with the question of increase in population of the productive sort and the facilities afforded it for the application of its intelligence and industry.
It is probable that in the straitened financiai 
conditions which may prevail for some years forward the question of capital for the development of agriculture may be of paramount importance, and it is our intention to inquire carefully during the coming recess into this most important subject, with a view, if desirable in the public interest, to supplementing by federal aid existing facilities in this connection.
I gathered from those remarks that at last out Government, and especially the Finance Minister, had awakened to the fact that agriculture was the basis of our prosperity, and upon the development of that industry depended the ability of our country to carry those vast burdens which are laid upon us by reason of the war. I remembered when he was speaking in this strain that the Government of which he is a member had put an embargo upon the export of horses to the United States, and upon the export of wool and of hay; I remembered that that Government had seized thirteen and a half million bushels of the farmers' wheat at a low price; I remembered that on every occasion previous to the minister making his remarks his Government had considered the farming industry as the industry to be exploited in the interests of every other interest there might be in the country, that might claim for a moment the favourable consideration of the Government. And so I must say it was with pleasure I heard that the Government not only realized the importance of the farming industry, but that they proposed-at some time in the future, I noticed-to come to the assistance of that industry with a view to increasing the results of the labour of those engaged in it. To-day when a question is brought up in this House the answer to which involves an increase in the earnings of the agricultural population, and which, by reason of that increase of earnings, involves an expansion and development of the industry of agriculture resulting from the prosperity of those engaged in it, I find my hon. friend spending two solid hours in proving, to his own satisfaction and with the enthusiastic support of his friends behind him, that this resolution should not be agreed to; that the farmer of the West should not have the opportunity for better markets that would come to him under the terms of the resolution; that instead of the Government being the means by which the farmer is to get more money with which to carry on his enterprise, the Government is to be the means to prevent him from getting, that money; and whereas, my hon. friend's proposal for assistance was for some time in the future, his action in pre-

vention of profit is in the immediate present.
My hon. friend paid careful attention to the question of markets in the United States for Canada's wheat. He saw, year in and year out, the market records which proved, as absolutely as the multiplication table can prove, that the market price in the United States was better than the market price in Canada; that if the Canadian farmer had access to that market, he would get the benefit of that price; but he argued again and again to prove that 'what was, plainly and evidently so, could not possibly be so. He reminded me very much of the elderly and unsophisticated agriculturist who had an opportunity of attending a wild beast show which contained, amongst other wonders, a giraffe. This ancient farmer, after examining the different attractions, finally halted in front of this giraffe and examined him carefully with his eye, looked over his height and width and spots and other peculiarities, and finally turned away and gave his verdict in these words: ".There ain t no [DOT] such animal."
Now, either there is a market in the United States for our wheat _ or there is not. If there is a market at better prices than we can get at home, it would be good not only for the farmer, but foT the whole population of the country to have that market, because I have my hon. friend's authority for saying " of the resources of Canada, the greatest and most fundamental is agriculture." Therefore, if the farmer of the prairie West can have the market price for his wheat improved by access to the market of the United States, then not only does he benefit, but every industry and interest throughout the Dominion of Canada benefits; and if we argue on the ground of patriotism, the ability of the Canadian people to carry the burden of taxation necessarily laid upon them by and through this war can and will be the more easily borne. If any government of any country, at any time, ever had a duty that lay upon them more heavily than any other, it is the duty as set out by my hon. friend in the paragraph which I have read from his address of yesterday. If there is an opportunity of improving the markets for the produce of the West, our greatest industry, it is the duty of the Government to see that that opportunity is taken advantage of.
My hon. friend says: We must not sell our wheat in the States this year at a good price, because perhaps we shall not be able
to sell it there at as good a price next year; that is, because we can get a dollar a bushel for our wheat this year, we should not take it, because next year we may not be able to get more than ninety cents. I commend the Minister of Finance to a study of the logic of his own expressions and I think he will agree that if he is to be taken at his (word, according to his own argument, which, of course, he is not to be, the Premier made a mistake when he selected his Minister of Finance.
Either we better our position by reason of the American market, or we do not; if we do not better our position, then our wheat will not go South, and that danger feared by my hon. friend to the traffic of our railroads, that danger that was so remarkably brought to his attention by men employed on the railroads, does not occur. If the market is not there, the wheat will not go there, and our Canadian railroads will still carry the traffic. If the market is there, and the wheat does go there and the (Canadian railroads do not get the traffic, it will be because the Canadian farmer gets a better price for his wheat. There is no escape from the condition. The difference between my hon. friend and his Government, and his followers, and us on this side of the House is this, that he is prepared, as he and his colleagues and his supporters have always been prepared, to set the interests of the railroads, or the millers, or the manufacturers or any other industry under heaven against that of the farmers. Again, I call attention to his statement that agriculture is the basic industry of our country.
Is it not a fact that the Government of which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) was a member was willing to bonus the millers under the reciprocity agreement?

I am not arguing on the
reciprocity agreement at this time, but I may say that that agreement would have given the Canadian farmer exactly that which we are demanding for him to-day, and which this Government could give him if it would; but it will not. _

But it would not have
given the Canadian farmer free flour, which the hon. gentleman considers important.

That is not the argument at all. This resolution relates to free wheat. The reciprocity proposal would have given the Canadian farmer free access to the American market for his wheat, which

would have been of great benefit to him, as was admitted by the Minister of Finance in the statement which he himself read. And this Government is able to give that to the Canadian farmer to-day, but it will not.
The Minister of Finance was deeply interested in the mixed farming industry. I do not recall a time, since I first took an interest in the public life of this Dominion, when the western settler was not advised to go into mixed farming, and when, from time to time, other sage and similar advice was not tendered him. I represent a constituency where the people are, and always have been, engaged in mixed farming. Let me . suggest to the Minister of Finance and to his colleagues that approximately twenty-five to thirty per cent of the so-called Prairie West is, and always has been, engaged in mixed farming, and that possibly the people there are not so much in need of either information or advice as to their business as some of our friends seem to think. When the hon. gentleman suggests that the mixed farmer is opposed to the grain farmer getting justice at the hands of this or some other Government, then, speaking for the mixed farmer, as I am entitled to do, I say the hon. gentleman misunderstands the position. The mixed farmer of the West raises the requirements for his stock on his own farm, in large measure. It is because the country is more suited to the production of that class of product that the farmer there is a mixed farmer.
The hon. minister was anxious that the mixed farmer should have the benefit of the bran and shorts that would come from the grinding of wheat, and he warned everybody that if free wheat to the United States were granted there would be no expansion of the milling industry in the West. Perhaps he is under the impression that there is not any milling industry in the West to-day. Perhaps he does not know that the big end of the milling industry in Canada is in the West, that the West grinds more wheat than it consumes. So, there is no injury to be done to the West by reason of the non-expansion of the milling industry. The milling industry of the West, if it is to expand, must expand by reason of its export market and not by reason of its local market.
The minister warned everybody-and I think this was one of the great national evils of which he spoke-that if this resolu-
tion carried it would be possible for the millers of the 'United States to get possession of the hard wheat of the Northwest and they would be able to mix it with their own softer American wheat and put the flour upon the European market in competition with the products of our mills. He considered that to be an evil to be guarded against by voting down this resolution. But in the beginning of his remarks he told us that under the law of the United States to-day the American miller can import our wheat and, having ground it into flour and exported it, can get a drawback of 99 peT cent of the duty. So, he was not fair to the House and the country when in his later remarks he suggested that if we passed this resolution the Canadian miller would cease to be protected against the competition of the American miller using Canadian grain in foreign markets. He was at that moment using an argument which was absolutely contradicted by the statement he made in the beginning of his remarks.

The hon. member is
entirely mistaken. The statement of the Finance Minister Was that on wheat shipped and ground in bond the United States miller could get a rebate of 99 per cent of the duty, but he cannot mix that wheat with American wheat in grinding. It must go through with its identity preserved.

Then, the case is just that much worse for the Minister of Finance. The American millers are able to go on the foreign market, not with a mixed product, but with flour made entirely of our Northwest wheat, and so can compete with our millers on equal terms.

That is right; so they
can.

So, I maintain that my
interpretation of the statement of the Minister of Finance is absolutely correct, and again I say that the argument he made in the latter part of his remarks is absolutely contradicted by the statement he made in the beginning of his remarks. The fact is, that the Minister of Finance or any other man who argues, ox tries ito argue that it is in the interests of the Dominion of Canada that our farmers should be excluded from an adjacent advantageous market, is arguing against the facts and necessarily must be guilty of contradictions and lapses such as this.
The Minister of Finance is sure that if the United States duty were

taken away, either by action of this Government, or by action of the United States Government without action on our part, the result would be an equalization of the prices between Minneapolis and Fort William. It is our hope that that would be the case; what we wish is that the prices shall be equalized. We want to get the benefit of whatever milling advantages there are in Minneapolis. We are entitled to that if we can get it, and if the policy laid down by the minister in his speech of yesterday is correct. Why is he so insistent that the removal of the duty would not be of benefit to the Canadian wheat grower, when he knows that exactly the same argument was made in regard to the producer of Canadian cattle and Canadian hogs? I have no doubt that my hon. friend, when he was championing the cause of high tariff against reciprocity in 1911; used exactly these arguments. Since then the United States have taken off the duty on hogs and cattle, and prices have been measurably equalized. The result has been that the Canadian price has come up, and the Canadian producer is getting the benefit to-day of access to the American market for his cattle and his hogs, notwithstanding the fact that the United States exports both cattle and hogs to the European market in very large numbers. I fancy they export to the European market more cattle and hogs than Canada exports to the United States. But that does not concern us. If by reason of our conditions as to transportation or quality of products or as to proximity to market, we get a better price by sending our goods to the United States, what matters it where the United States send their goods? That is no concern of ours.
There is another product of the West that in our part of the country is more important than wheat, that is oats. Some years ago the American duty on oats was cut down to six cents a bushel. The duty before that time had been prohibitive. But when the duty was cut down to six cents a bushel, our measurable access to the markets of the United States saved the situation to the farmers of Alberta in respect to the crop of three years ago. We sold many millions of bushels of oats to the United States in that year, and this saved us from having practically to give our oats away.
In view of these facts, in view of the contradictions into which my hon. friend's arguments necessarily lead him, there is
nothing to be said against the desirability of the Canadian farmer securing access to the United States market for his wheat free of duty. But we have the other side of the question.
My hon. friend has been frank with the House and with the country. While he has talked on behalf of the Canadian farmer and of Imperial interests and desires to convey the impression that it would be dangerous to the future of the Empire, in its consolidation after the war, to allow the farmer to get five cents more for his wheat at the present time, as a matter of fact he has informed the House and the country that the reason the Government will not agree to give the western farmer free wheat is because it is bound to maintain on behalf of the Canadian milling industry that protection which it enjoys at the present time. That is the reason he gives, that is the only reason he gives that can be understood- and it, of course, can be easily understood. The milling industry of Canada is an important and desirable industry. Many parts of the country are well adapted to that industry and we are glad to see it flourishing; but why should the milling industry flourish at the expense of the agricultural industry? If it has to be a choice between the two, if. there is not room in the same country for both to flourish on equal terms, then certainly the agricultural industry, on the authority of my hon. friend, should be the premier concern of the Government of the day. Certainly if either one has to take second place, that which is minor should take second place, not that which is major. And yet my hon. friend has urged here that it is the minor industry that must be protected to the loss and cost of many millions to the major industry. How, I ask, is this country to achieve prosperity through the development of its agricultural resources by any such policy as that?
This country is well adapted to the milling industry up to a certain point. For the supply of our own demands, there is no country in the world better situated than this Dominion of Canada for the establishment and maintenance of a successful and profitable flour milling industry. There is jjp other country that has the wheat and the water powers in such abundance and railway facilities equal to ours. Then there is no reason why the Canadian milling industry should require an extraordinary measure of protection at

the hands of this Government. It is entitled, no doubt, to whatever measure of protection would naturally fall to it under a revenue tariff: I would not suggest at all that it should not have the benefit of that measure of protection. But that the great farming industry should be penalized to the extent of twelve and a half million dollars on its crop this year because of the milling industry, I say is not good business for any country by any Government. The milling industry is a good industry, but it is not wdrth the money.
How does the hon. gentleman figure out the twelve and a half million dollars?	[DOT]

I heard the Minister of Finance say that we had 250,000,000 bushels of'wheat for export. I also heard him read figures which would lead me to believe that the United States prices were at least five cents a bushel better on the average than our prices here. I figure that would work out about twelve and a half million dollars.
But the hon. member for Assiniboia said the Canadian farmer would not get that.

Then I have to disagree with the hon. member for Assiniboia, because I think that, conditions being as they are, the Canadian farmer would get the benefit. I do not pretend that conditions are always as favourable as they are to-day. There is no doubt that the advantage of the United States market depends on the conditions as they exist from time to time. But it will be noticed in the figures that the minister read during the- afternoon, that whenever the Winnipeg price was higher than the Minneapolis price, in any year or at any time of any year, it was a time when the Canadian farmer did not have any important quantity of wheat to sell; that whenever the Canadian farmer had a large surplus of wheat to dispose of, in any year, or at any time of year, then the 'Minneapolis price in every case was much better than the Canadian price.
. Mr. SCHAFFNER: That was not so about the 25th of September last year. For about three weeks wheat was higher in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis last fall.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say that there was no time or season when wheat was higher in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis.	,
I said there were times and seasons when wheat was higher in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis, but that these were times and seasons when the Canadian farmer did not have the wheat to sell.
He had this year.
Oh no, he had not.
At the end of September?

Oh no, his shipments
were held back in September, he was not getting his wheat forward. That is why the price was different, and my hon. friend knows it.
Why could he not get it forward?
It was not threshed.
I think the hon. gentleman is wrong on that point. I say that in September the price of wheat was higher in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis, and the conditions were all right then.

I will stand by the position I have taken, and I think it will be agreed that the only times when wheat is higher in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis are the times and seasons when there is a minimum of Canadian wheat coming forward, and a maximum of American wheat going forward. There is no doubt about that. Does my hon. friend suggest that the fact that there was a period in September when the price of wheat was higher in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis is a reason why this resolution should not be agreed to?

I do not; I was
simply correcting what I believed to be a misstatement, unintentional no doubt. If my hon. friend takes the three last months of last year, October, November and December, he will find that the price was higher in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis, and certainly wheat was coming forward then.

Undoubtedly, but the fact that my hon. friend does not consider that as a reason why the resolution should not be supported is evidence, I take it, that he agrees with me as to the general condition, that the Canadian farmer would benefit by the adoption of this resolution.
I turn from the question of wheat to the question of flour. We have had a commission acting for some years in Canada. I do not know what it has cost, and I do not

know what it has done. But there has been a commission on the high cost of living. I have noticed that from month to month and from year to yeaij-there have been exceptions to the rule, but I maintain that it is the rule nevertheless-the cost of living in Canada has been climbing, and nobody will say that the price of flour is not an important item in the cost of living. If we have enormous additional burdens of taxation to carry because of the war, and we have, it is surely one of the [DOT] greatest of the national interests which should concern this Government to see that other burdens upon the shoulders of our people are lightened as much as posible. If we are going to tax the people to pay the interest on war indebtedness, as we must pay it, surely it is our business to so adjust our trade and our affairs as to permit the people to pay that tax by relieving them of as many other burdens as possible. To maintain the milling industry in its present position, not only the producer must be sacrificed, but the consumer must continue to pay. There you find the great objection that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance had to agreeing to this resolution; it would relieve the consumer in some measure of the burden that he carries at the present time, and would thereby enable him the better to carry the burden of governmental taxation that must necessarily be laid upon his shoulders. The producer on the one hand, the consumer on the other, and the miller between; he takes from the farmer, and from the consumer, and the Government stands behind him and says: Yes, we are going to stand behind him. And the minister suggested that he is doing this in the national interest. I do not wish to speak otherwise than with the highest respect for the Minister of Finance, but after the deliverance which hb made yesterday in regard to the greatest interest that can concern us at this time, I say that his special pleading on behalf of the milling industry of Canada to-day was not worthy of the sentiments that he placed on Hansard yesterday.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance wanted to know who it was that fixed the market price of wheat in the West, and he used the name of the' Grain Grower^ Grain Company. He received vociferous applause from his supporters when be used that name, and he seemed to think that it supplied a convincing answer to every argument and statement of fact made by the hon. member for Assiniboia. If my hon.
friend would look at the last annual statement of the Ogilvie Milling Company, he would find that a large part of the $1,600,000 of profits, which the company claims to have made last year, was made not out of milling at all, but out of the buying of grain. It is a fact that the great milling industries of Canada in large measure control the market price of grain in the West. Why should they not? They have the chance of working up their purchases in their mills as much as they desire, and of exporting the balance. As a matter of fact there is no doubt to-day that the great milling combines of Canada are combines to control the purchase of wheat in the West, just as much as they are combines to control the sale of flour in the East.
Will the hon. gentleman say that the milling companies in Canada buy as much western wheat as does the Grain Growers' Grain Company?
I do not say that, but I do say that the milling industry of Canada is not, in effect, a competitor of the Grain Growers' Grain Company in the buying of wheat.
Is there a combination between them ?
I could not say that. I am satisfied that there is a combination amongst the millers and 1 am a little afraid that there is an understanding between the millers and the buyers.
Will you except the Grain Growers' Grain Company?

I do not know why that
name should appeal to my hon. friends. The Grain Growers' Grain Company is in the grain buying business, the same as the Ogilvie Milling Company is in the milling business.
It is composed of grain-growers only.

It makes' no difference
what it is composed of, it is a business enterprise and it is carried on for the profit of the members of that enterprise. If a market condition exists, created by the legislation of this Government and assisted by the millers combine, which is also the creation of this Government, are the Grain Growers' Grain Company expected, because they are farmers buying grain, not to take some measure of advantage of the situation thus created? My hon. friend (Mr. Wright)

I
is a farmer himself and he does not claim to be an angel.
This company was formed for the express purpose of coming to the rescue of the farmers of the Northwest.

I am not sure that they
have not achieved some measure of success in the fulfilment of the purpose for which they were formed. The antagonism with which my hon. friends opposite receive the mention of the name from this side of the House would lead me to believe that they had. But never mind about that-I say that the Grain Growers' Grain Company is a business enterprise. They are taking, and they are entitled to take, whatever profits they can by reason of the conditions which this Government, and the combines existing under it, have set up throughout the western country. I believe that they have ameliorated these conditions, but it would be too much to expect that they had absolutely ignored them.

Is the hon. gentleman's argument, that the Grain Growers' Grain Company are really in a position to pay a much larger price for western wheat than they do, but knowing that they are in the position to make a big profit, they refuse to pay the legitimate value of the wheat?

I do not know why my
hon. friend should suggest these words to me. I have already given him the view which I hold in regard to the Grain Growers' Grain Company.
Is the way I express it right or not?

I think my hon. friend
will have to take the expression as I give it and not the expression he gives it. If he will be good enough to do that I will be satisfied and I hope he will. I do not wish to delay the House longer in this matter. The appeal made by the minister as an excuse for not dealing with this question, that at some time in the future, when this war is over, there will have to be a readjustment of inter-imperial trade relationships, may have some bearing upon the matter in his mind that we on this side of the House do not understand. But I would respectfully isuggest that any proposals, any claim for special consideration of inter-imperial trade obligations and preferences, comes with rather, bad grace from the Minister of Finance in a Government which only last session increased the duties against British products coming into Cana-

da to the amount of 51 per cent. It will be enough for this Government, and this Parliament, [DOT] to consider the condition in which we find ourselves to-day and the condition that we will be called upon to face during the immediately following years. What will happen after this war is over may take care of itself. What we have to do is to see that the war is won, and that our country is in a proper position after the war is won. We have, as the minister said yesterday, to meet enormous obligations already accrued. We have to meet still more enormous obligations already in sight and we know not what further obligations we will have to meet before we will have occasion to consider what will take place after the war is over. Is this a time when tribute should be laid on the farmer, on the great producing industry of the West, on the one hand, and on the labouring man of the eastern cities, on the other, in the interest of a single industry in Canada? There may have been times and occasions in the history of our country when we could afford to sacrifice the larger for the smaller interest, but on the word of the minister himself, this is not such a time, this is not such an occasion. This is an occasion when the producer on the one hand, and the consumer on the other, should receive the benefit of every advantage that this Government, by its legislation, can confer upon them. No greater advantage lies in the hands of this Government to confer than to give, by acceding to .this resolution, to the farmer of the West a better price for his wheat, and to the consumer of the East, a lower price for his flour.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming from western 'Canada, as I do, I naturally have a very deep and lasting interest in everything that can possibly appertain to the welfare of the people of that portion of our Dominion. I was a little surprised at the statement of my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) regarding the export of wheat in bond to the United States. If my hon. friend has no clearer idea of the true conditions than that which he expressed in this particular case, then I am bound to say that he has a very limited knowledge of the grain situation. The case as stated by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) is absolutely correct. Wheat shipped in bond through the United States can be ground by any miller in the United States, the flour, the product of that wheat, can be exported to Great Britain, and the United States miller can get his drawback

of 99 per cent; or, in other words, the duty payable on the wheat which was used by the miller in the United States is simply one dollar per thousand bushels. That is the United States law as it exists to-day, but the proposed resolution before this House is a very different thing. It provides for the opening of the American market and the mixing of Canadian and American wheat, and thereby exporting it, after it is turned into flour, in competition with the Canadian farmers' wheat in the market of Great Britain. That is a sample of the arguments which have fallen from the lips of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House since the beginning of this debate. They are evidently not posted in any way whatever upon the conditions as they actually exist.
I am free to admit that the resolution before us concerns a question which in past years, especially in Western Canada, has excited a very considerable amount of interest, and I agree that any formal proposal from our neighbours to the south in regard to that question is entitled to our most respectful and careful consideration. But we must always remember that the Underwood tariff, on which the proposal now before us is based, was framed by those whose first and only duty was the preparation of a tariff which, in their judgment, would carry with it advantages in some form or other to the people of the United States, whom they were undertaking to serve. I am sure that no hon. member in this House would say that the provision in the Underwood tariff giving us free access to the American market, on certain conditions, was made for the purpose of giving the Canadian producer of Western Canada any special advantage. It, therefore, becomes our special duty to give this question most earnest and careful consideration, in order to ascertain whether there is justification for the statement thet the acceptance of this proposal would carry with it advantage to the farming community and to the people of Canada generally. But let me first express my regret at the very extravagant and unreasonable statements that have been made on this subject during the course of this debate. In my humble judgment this subject should be discussed in reason and in fairness from all points of view. It is quite true that there have been occasions in the past when the farmers of the western provinces did not receive full value for their products. To my mind, one of the principal reasons for that is that in the early days
we had the idea that we should set a very high standard for our wheat, and we carried that idea out. It is true that the farmers have lost a considerable amount of money in the past on that account; and. in my humble judgment, it is equally true that they have lost a considerable amount of money by reason of the fact that we have not had a sample market. These, to my mind, are the two principal causes of monetary loss to the farmers of Western Canada in past years. In order to make myself perfectly clear on these two important points, and in order that the House may better understand the true situation, perhaps I cannot do better than read the opinions of a very important commission which was appointed by the Government of the province of Saskatchewan, and which reported in 1914. The purpose for which they were appointed is set out in the Order in Council as follows: "To examine into ways and means for bettering the position of Saskatchewan grain on the European markets." The commissioners made a very . exhaustive examination of the subject; they spent months and months in Europe, visiting almost every wheat centre there, and in 1914, presented their report. This is what the commissioners say in regard to trading on sample at Winnipeg or Fort William:
It is, intended to create a sample market at Winnipeg and at Fort William. Considered theoretically and viewed from certain angles trading on sample is the ideal method. What the Saskatchewan farmer should ask, however, is: What will be the effect of sample trading on the price realized by the farmers for the crop of Saskatchewan? To consider the possible effect on a small proportion of the crop while Ignoring the probable effect upon the general level of values would be shortsighted. Consider these facts:
1.	The surplus of wheat over and above Canadian millers' requirements which must export determines Jthe prices at which our crop will be sold.
Here the commission is in conflict with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver). The report continues:
The competition of exporters forces the millers to pay at least export price for wheat, while, on the other hand, there is always enough wheat, arid usually enough of each grade to render it unnecessary for the millers to pay more than a slight premium over export price for what they need. Therefore, the all important consideration is to maintain the integrity or standard of our export grades.
2.	Any condition that creates or maintains confidence in our wheat abroad helps to raise or to sustain prices that are hid for opr wheat from abroad.
3.	Higher or sustained bids from abroad (relatively, of course, to the bids being made for the wheat of other countries) mean not only



a higher price for the surplus that is exported, but for all that is milled at home for which the millers must outbid the exporters.
4.	In exactly the same way any condition that weakens or destroys confidence in our wheat abroad will lower the prices at which our entire crop will be sold, because lowering the prices that exporters can afford to pay for it.
5.	At the present time Canadian wheat enjoys the confidence of the British and the continental trade, partly on its merits, but partly because it can be depended upon to be delivered as represented.
5. We should do nothing that will imperil that confidence unless we are sure that the financial gain to the producers that will result *will outweigh the financial loss that would follow all impairment of foreign confidence in the integrity of our certificate.
I entirely agree with the views of this commission, because they represent, to my mind, the responsible facts of the case, and the commissioners give good reasons why, in thedr opinion, we should go slow in the establishment of that sample market. It is due to that, in my opinion, that the farmers of Western Canada have suffered great loss. When I was in Winnipeg some time last autumn, I happened 'to meet in the Grain Exchange a farmer who had just . shipped in a car of flax. He had got his certificate from the grain inspector and his flax graded No. 2 whereas he thought it should have graded No. 1. He had eleven hundred odd bushels of flax in his car and he complained very bitterly about the grade which he had been given. Under the law he had a right to appeal to the survey board of the Grain Exchange as against the certificate handed to him by the inspector. He did this; the appeal was heard by the survey board, and they were just about to decide that the Inspector was wrong, and that the farmer should have a higher grade for his car of flax when the inspector suggested that it might be well for them to weigh the flax in order to see if it came within the weight prescribed by this Parliament which would entitle him to a certificate of No. 1 for his car. When the flax was weighed it was found to be just half a pound too light to come under the standard as provided by law, and therefore that farmer lost that particular grade on his car of eleven hundred bushels of flax, which meant to him a loss of thirty cents a bushel or something over {300; whereas /if he had had a sample market, he would have been able to sell that particular car at probably one or two cents a bushel less than the price of the particular grade which he had hoped to receive.
The same thing applies so far as high

grade standards Eire concerned. We in Western Canada for twenty-five long years have held the idea of sticking firmly to a high grade standard, believing, as the people and the farmers especially believe, that the day would soon come when they would reap their reward and when they would be able to establish in the markets of the world the great advantage that our wheat possesses as compared with the wheat of any other country that competes with us. A great effort has been made and a large amount of money has been lost in maintaining that particular position on behalf of the farmers. I would like to quote again from this report of the commissioners what they have to say on the matter of the high standards, and I am doing this simply in order to bring to the notice of the House the actual facts as they are understood by the farming community of Western Canada:
The Canadian certificate is highly thought of in the world's markets. It enjoys a better reputation than any other certificate. United States grain is exported under a variety of certificates emanating from different and unrelated sources, such as state authorities, boards of trade, chambers of commerce and port authorities. The reputation enjoyed by these certificates in importing countries is not such as to commend to Canadians any change in the source of the Canadian certificate. Seaboard inspections in particular are not popular among importing merchants.
Because it is imported on a dependable certificate, Canadian grain is dealt in on a smaller margin of profit than the grain of any other exporting country. Three-eights of a cent per bushel is the profit the importing merchants of Liverpool and London calculate on their Canadian business as compared for instance with as much as two and a quarter cents per bushel on Russian business owing to various elements of uncertainty connected "With that trade. The importing trade makes little or no distinction in its bids as between grain shipped through United States ports in bond and grain shipped through ail Canadian channels. Importers are satisfied that the integrity of the grades is preserved as well one way as the other. Liverpool prefers Canadian grain ex New York to that ex Montreal, if anything. Some markets claim that spring and summer arrivals are not of as high a standard as those of the fall and winter, hut make no distinction as between routes. On the other hand, the trade does not like to purchase Canadian wheat with only a United States seaboard inspection certifying the wheat to be of some specified grade but of " Canadian origin."
Now, this is the position to which I wish to draw the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite, because it is a very important one and one that interests the people of Western Canada in particular. I intend to discuss this matter later on, but I wish to say a word before six o'clock to some of my

hon. friends who have been dealing with the question of the prices of wheat at Winnipeg, Minneapolis, and elsewhere. I am indeed more than surprised at the extravagant statements that have been made first of all by my hon. friend from Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff), and then by others who have followed him. He told us, the other night for example, that which was quoted by the Minister of Finance to-day, that wheat in Winnipeg was seven or eight cents cheaper than in Minneapolis and that when it reached Liverpool it was seven or eight cents higher. I would like to ask my hon. friend if he believes that the Grain Growers' Grain Association, which embraces thousands and thousands of the best farmers of the West, and which was formed for the express purpose of .guarding the interests of the farmers of the West, is guilty of wrong-doing against the farming community. My hon. friend in his speech the other night when dealing with this particular point used the following language:
But what do we find when the wheat got to Liverpool? Instead of the Manitoba farmer getting seven or eight cents less a bushel than the American farmer, he received from the Liverpool merchant from six to eight cents a bushel more than the American farmer, and that cannot be denied by any one who knows anything about the grain trade. Why should there be this difference? Why should every man who grows wheat in Canada be crucified to the extent of ten cents a bushel on his wheat?

If my hon. friend will
allow me, I pointed out to the Minister of Finance this afternoon-perhaps my hon. friend was not in the House then-that I 'did not use that language at all. It is a mis-quotation on the part of Hansard and I have corrected it, and my hon. friend will see in the Revised Hansard what I said.
Will my hon. friend deny that he used the word " crucified " with respect to the farmers of the West?
No, that is the absolute truth.
Will he say that the Grain Growers' Grain Company are crucifying their fellow-farmers in Western Canada?

I did not use the name of the Grain Growers' Grain Company in that connection. I said that my constituents, for ten or eleven months out of the year, could take their wheat across the line, if it were free of duty, and get from ten to sixteen cents a bushel more for it than they can get at home. That is the truth, and I stand by it, and state that under
the present system the farmers are being crucified.

That has no bearing on
the quotation I have been reading, which the hon. member says he stands behind- that the farmers are being crucified to the extent he stated. Will he say that Grain Growers' Grain Company are crucifying the farmers of Western Canada, for they are to-day the largest dealers and exporters of grain in the Dominion of Canada? They have shipped, I believe, something like 100,000,000 bushels of wheat.

Does the hon. gentleman want an answer? The Grain Growers' Grain Company are more persistent than any other people in their demand for enabling our wheat to go into the American market free of duty. Both the Grain Growers' Association and the Grain Growers' Grain Company are demanding that. And if the Government will put wheat on the free list and let the Canadian farmer have free access to the American market they will satisfy the Grain Growers' Associations of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and the Grain Growers' Grain Company as well.

My hon. friend is trying to get away from the question. He made a distinct statement that the farmers of the West were being crucified in the sale of their wheat. Now the Grain Growers' Grain Company trade and deal in the wheat of the western farmer, almost in its entirety.
How did the Ogilvies make that $1,000,000?
The Grain Growers' Grain Company are handling over half of it in Western Canada to-day.

Does the hon. minister
deny the statement of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) as to the difference in the price as judged by the Liverpool market?

I do not deny that the price is higher in Liverpool. I say the price has been higher and is higher to-day. The prices that come into play and that we have to consider are the prices of cash wheat to-day. What does that represent when we compare the prices of cash wheat? These are the facts. Cash wheat to-day at Fort William and every other point in Canada is at a premium over the May option. Now, the option is regulated largely by the position of the wheat, the closer to the seaboard

the higher the premium, because the people of Europe want our wheat. It is true, the premium at Fort William may he Only five cents a bushel over the May option to-day, But if you have that wheat at Buffalo or some other point east of the Great Lakes, the premium on Canadian wheat over the May option is over fifteen cents a bushel. But on the American side what are the conditions? On that side, at any port on the seaboard, you can buy cash wheat at a discount of over five and a half cents a bushel. Come with me to New York, and you can stand on the docks and see Canadian wheat going to Liverpool at a price representing from twenty to twenty-five cents a bushel more than wheat from the United States.
Did the Canadian farmer get twenty-five cents a bushel more for it?

The Canadian farmer is
getting a good deal more for his wheat this year than the American farmer is getting for his, notwithstanding the statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite. The extravagant statements they put forth do not agree with the facts. Every person knows that in * trading in wheat there is no wide margin for the trader, for there are too many in the business and the profit is limited by competition. The fact is that Canadian wheat commands a price at the American seaboard of from t.wenty to twenty-five cents a bushel more than the American wheat. That is one of the reasons why I say this House would fail in its duty to the farming community of Western Canada if it did not reject the resolution of my hon. friend.
I have a good deal more to say, and it is now six o'clock. I hope to finish my remarks on this subject at a future sitting.
At six o'clock, the House adjourned, without motion put, pursuant to rule.
Thursday, February 17, 1916.
